opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, when I was interviewing, FAIR felt almost like a utopia for researchers. The model was very bottom-up: you weren't handed a product roadmap or told "this quarter you'll ship this feature." The idea was that you hire really strong people, give them a lot of freedom and compute, and trust that good research will come out of it. It was much closer to an academic lab than a typical corporate R&D group, but with resources most universities couldn't match.

What struck me most was the openness. Publishing was the default, open-sourcing code was the default, and people talked to each other across teams very freely. You could walk up to someone whose papers you'd been reading for years and just start a conversation. That culture was a big part of why I wanted to go there.

At the same time, I remember thinking, even then, that this kind of model depends on a certain balance. Freedom is wonderful, but it also means you have to set your own direction, and not everyone thrives in that. And for the company, there's always an implicit question of how this research eventually connects back to the larger mission. In those years the answer was mostly "long-term impact, be patient," and leadership seemed genuinely committed to that. For a young researcher, it was about as good an environment as you could ask for: a place to take risks, work on problems you believed in, and not worry too much about short-term payoff.

r001.rationale: The candidate says FAIR was much closer to an academic lab than a typical corporate R&D group, describing researcher freedom and a bottom-up model.

fable-5.1.text:
When I interviewed at FAIR, around 2016 or 2017, what struck me most was how much it felt like an academic department sitting inside a company, but one that had removed almost all the friction academics normally deal with. Yann LeCun had designed it very deliberately in the Bell Labs tradition: hire people who are already excellent, give them compute and freedom, don't tell them what to work on, and trust that good things come out. There was no mandate to tie your research to a product roadmap. Open publication and open-sourcing weren't just tolerated, they were the default expectation.

Coming from a PhD, that was very appealing, because the alternative paths each had a cost. Staying in academia meant spending a huge fraction of your time writing grants and managing a lab with limited GPUs. Joining a product team meant your research agenda would be shaped by quarterly goals. FAIR seemed to promise the best of both: industrial resources with academic autonomy.

At the same time, even during the interview, I could see the tension built into that model. If a lab is funded by a company but not asked to deliver anything to that company, its existence depends on continued goodwill and on the belief that fundamental research pays off on a long enough horizon. Yann was very explicit that FAIR's value to Facebook was partly about talent and reputation, not just technology transfer. That works beautifully when the company is growing and confident. I remember thinking it was a kind of bet, and I was happy to take that bet, because the people were extraordinary and the culture of sharing ideas freely, both internally and with the outside world, was something I hadn't seen anywhere else at that scale.

So my view then was mostly admiration, with a small question mark about how long a model like that could stay stable. In hindsight, both the admiration and the question mark turned out to be justified.

r001.rationale: The response describes FAIR as feeling like an academic department inside a company, with academic autonomy and few usual academic constraints, which characterizes it as operating essentially like a university.

astra-6.text: At the time, I was trying to understand how FAIR balanced open-ended research with being part of a company. For me, the key question was how that worked in practice: how researchers chose their problems, how they collaborated, and what counted as success. That was the lens through which I viewed its operating model during the interview.

r001.rationale: The response describes FAIR as balancing open-ended research with being part of a company, but does not characterize it as operating essentially like a university.

sol-6.1.text: At the time, my impression was that FAIR operated a lot like an academic research lab, but within a company. Researchers had considerable freedom to choose problems and pursue longer-term ideas, without necessarily having to connect every project to a product right away. To me, the appeal was that combination: an open research environment, strong colleagues, and the resources to explore ambitious questions.

r001.rationale: The response says FAIR operated “a lot like an academic research lab” within a company, conveying that its operating model was essentially university-like.
